content.text:
Yes—**npm just landed, and Python packages are a sensible next step.**

Recent PRs establish the foundation:

- [#13031](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13031): complete lockfile generation, including platform artifacts and checksums.
- [#13128](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13128): committed versions remain installable during the release-age cooling window.
- **[#13131](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13131), merged today:** npm tools installed through embedded aube now store their **full transitive dependency graph** in `mise.lock` revision 2 and replay it with frozen installs. Existing lockfiles opt in through `mise lock --upgrade`; `mise lock --bump npm:cowsay` refreshes dependencies even when cowsay’s version stays unchanged.

For Python, there are two different cases:

| What | Current support |
|---|---|
| Python interpreter (`python`) | Already locks versions and supported prebuilt artifacts |
| Python CLI packages (`pipx:black`, etc.) | Pins the tool version, but dependencies still resolve during installation |

**I’d extend `pipx:` with uv-backed dependency locking next**, following the aube pattern:

1. Resolve the complete dependency set during `mise lock` and store it with artifact hashes.
2. Install that recorded set into the tool’s isolated environment.
3. Include the graph and Python interpreter compatibility in installation identity, so projects with different dependency locks don’t share the wrong environment.
4. Make `--locked` fail when the installer cannot honor the graph.

uv already provides universal resolution and compilation/synchronization of `requirements.txt` or `pylock.toml`, so we could delegate resolution to it. The main design work is Python-version/platform markers, extras, and source-build dependencies. [uv documentation](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/pip/compile/)

I’d initially scope this to **PyPI CLI tools installed through uv**, with explicit handling of unsupported Git/editable dependencies. Project dependencies would continue using their own `uv.lock` or `package-lock.json`.

content.text:
**Ruby is the strongest next candidate after Python.** For full dependency graphs in `mise.lock`, I’d rank them:

| Ecosystem | Opportunity |
|---|---|
| **Ruby (`gem:`)** | High value. Current installs pin the main gem but resolve dependencies afresh. We could preserve a Bundler lock and install an isolated bundle, with executable wrappers. [Bundler](https://bundler.io/guides/deploying.html) |
| **Rust (`cargo:`)** | Useful, but less urgent: mise already supports passing `--locked` to Cargo, which uses the crate’s published `Cargo.lock`. Storing a project-selected graph would add control over dependency refreshes without changing the tool version. [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-install.html) |
| **Go (`go:`)** | Lower priority. Dependencies already flow through the tool’s module metadata; I’d first audit what additional reproducibility a mise-owned graph would provide. |
| **.NET (`dotnet:`)** | Worth investigating, but needs a tool-specific design. NuGet project locking shouldn’t be assumed to work with `dotnet tool install`. [Microsoft](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-ca/dotnet/core/tools/dotnet-tool-install) |
| **PHP / Composer** | Technically a good fit because Composer already supports frozen dependency versions. But mise has no native Composer package backend, making this a larger feature. [Composer](https://getcomposer.org/doc/01-basic-usage.md) |

**Conda already has dependency locking** in the current backend: it records dependency package URLs/checksums and reinstalls from those records.

My order would be **Python → Ruby → Rust**, using each ecosystem’s native resolver and lock format. The shared mise machinery should handle storing those locks, distinguishing installations by their contents, and enforcing `--locked`.

<proposed_plan>
# Python dependency locking and the `pypi:` backend name

## Summary

Create one ready-for-review PR against current `main` titled `feat(pypi): lock Python tool dependencies with uv`.

Make `pypi:` the preferred name, retaining `pipx:` as a supported alias. Add portable dependency locking for PyPI CLI tools installed through uv, initially requiring published wheels.

## Implementation

- Canonicalize `pypi:` and `pipx:` to one backend identity. Preserve existing installations, aliases, registry mappings, and lockfile lookups without duplicate installs or filesystem migration. Use `pypi:` in new generated output, documentation, and diagnostics; keep the actual `pipx` executable/tool name unchanged.
- Introduce `pypi` settings names with legacy `pipx` aliases. Reject contradictory values for the same setting. Preserve existing environment-variable compatibility. Keep the old documentation URL working. Do not deprecate or warn on `pipx:`.
- Build on the merged npm graph implementation. Introduce lockfile revision 3 so older clients reject Python graphs instead of silently ignoring them. Preserve revisions 0–2 until explicit `mise lock --upgrade`.
- Store a lossless native uv lock and its synthetic project inputs under each Python tool entry. Resolve the exact package plus requested extras in an isolated, non-package project. Derive the supported Python range from package metadata, bounded by uv’s supported interpreter range; retain universal platform and Python markers.
- Use an installed uv executable, requiring uv 0.12.10 or newer initially. Generate locks without installing packages or executing source builds. Preserve index authentication and release-age policy without serializing credentials.
- Replay through `uv sync --frozen` into a mise-owned environment, prohibiting source builds. Validate the root requirement, extras, interpreter compatibility, and hashed wheel artifacts before accepting the installation. Expose the requested tool’s console scripts through mise’s existing bin-path mechanism.
- Include canonical graph contents, effective tool options, and interpreter compatibility identity in installation identity. Different graphs coexist; listings retain the ordinary package version.
- Reuse graphs on ordinary locking; `mise lock --bump pypi:<tool>` refreshes dependencies even when the root version is unchanged. Apply release-age policy during resolution, without re-resolving committed dependencies during installation.
- Fail clearly for missing or invalid revision-3 graphs, unavailable uv, incompatible interpreters, missing wheels, or attempts to consume a uv graph through standalone pipx. Retain legacy standalone-pipx and Git-source behavior outside graph locking. Reject nonempty free-form installer arguments for graph locking in this first version rather than silently ignoring their effects.

## Validation

- Test alias equivalence across parsing, settings, backend disabling, legacy lockfiles, existing installation discovery, and newly generated output.
- Test graph serialization, deterministic identity, upgrade behavior, unchanged-lock reuse, dependency bumps, extras, and Python/platform marker selection.
- Use controlled package fixtures to verify frozen installation despite newer upstream dependencies, checksum failures, missing wheels, unsupported options, and incompatible-installer errors.
- Execute installed console scripts on Unix and Windows; verify graph-specific coexistence and interpreter compatibility handling.
- Run focused Python and lockfile unit/e2e suites through the repository tasks, required lint fixes, and relevant documentation/schema generation and checks.

## PR and follow-through

- Document `pypi:` examples, the continuing `pipx:` alias, uv requirements, wheel-only coverage, and migration with `mise lock --upgrade`.
- Review the complete diff, open a non-draft PR against `main`, and include the required AI disclosure and actual validation results.
- Monitor current-head checks and reviews. Fix actionable feedback and failing checks, reply and resolve addressed threads, and repeat until checks pass and actionable feedback is settled.
- Leave the PR unmerged. Report any external blocker requiring user action.
</proposed_plan>
